plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000070), an original story: a teenage narrator's summer working for an aunt who tunes pianos, a visit to a widower who keeps his late wife's piano tuned, and the narrator first hearing the beats. Original fiction, so no outside facts; narrator's gender unspecified. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Ten items, several hard (cross-paragraph principle, figurative statement, final-gesture inference). Plus R069-03 (revision 2, key reworded) on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000069. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Beats
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, my mother arranged for me to work for her sister, Ines, who tuned pianos for a living. I had imagined spending those months at the community pool with my friends, and I let everyone know it. On the first morning, Ines handed me a canvas bag full of tools I could not name and said only, "Carry this. Don't drop the forks."

The forks, I learned, were tuning forks, and Ines owned a dozen of them, though she rarely used more than one. Our first stop was a church basement where an upright piano had been pushed against a damp wall for what looked like decades. Ines lifted the lid, played a single chord, and winced as if someone had stepped on her foot. To me it sounded like a piano. "Listen to the beats," she said, striking two keys together. I heard nothing but two notes. She did not explain further. She simply went to work, turning pins with a lever and stopping every few seconds to listen with her head tilted, as though the instrument were whispering.

For the first two weeks, I was mostly bored. I carried the bag, handed her mutes and felt strips when she held out her hand, and watched the clock on whatever wall was nearest. Ines did not seem to mind my silence; she was not much of a talker herself. At lunch she ate the same sandwich every day, cheese and pickles, and read paperback mysteries with the covers torn off. When I asked why she tore them off, she said she didn't like being told what to expect.

It was in the third week, in the living room of an elderly man named Mr. Okafor, that something shifted. His piano was old but well cared for, and while Ines worked, he sat in an armchair and told me that his late wife had played it every evening. "I don't play," he said. "But I like to know it's ready." Ines tuned for nearly two hours, longer than she had spent on any instrument that summer, though to my ears the piano had sounded fine when we arrived. When she finished, she played a slow piece I didn't recognize, and Mr. Okafor closed his eyes.

On the drive home, I asked her why she had taken so long on a piano no one played. She was quiet for a while. "He listens," she said finally. "That's someone playing it."

The next morning she handed me a fork and pointed at the A above middle C on an old practice piano in her garage. "Strike them both," she said. I did, and for the first time I heard it: a faint wavering, a slow pulse inside the sound, like two people walking almost but not quite in step. I turned the pin a fraction, and the pulse slowed. I turned it again, and it vanished. I looked up, expecting her to say something. She was already reading her mystery, but she had stopped turning the pages.

passages.title: The Door That Swung Both Ways
passages.text:
In the 1960s, the Soviet climate scientist Mikhail Budyko built a simple mathematical model of Earth's climate and found something unsettling. Ice reflects more sunlight than ocean or bare land does, so as ice sheets spread, the planet absorbs less heat, cools further, and grows still more ice. In Budyko's model, if the ice ever spread far enough toward the equator, this feedback would run away and the entire planet would freeze. Budyko did not believe this had ever happened. Once frozen, he reasoned, a white Earth would reflect so much sunlight that it could never thaw, and since Earth was plainly not frozen now, the runaway must never have begun.

Geologists, meanwhile, had a puzzle of their own. In rocks roughly 700 million years old, they kept finding deposits left by glaciers, jumbled mixtures of boulders and fine clay of the kind that ice sheets drop as they melt. Measurements of the rocks' ancient magnetism indicated that some of these deposits had formed near the equator. Some researchers suspected that the magnetic measurements were wrong; others proposed that Earth's axis had once been tilted so steeply that the tropics were colder than the poles. Neither explanation won many converts.

In 1992, the geologist Joseph Kirschvink offered a bolder answer in a short paper: perhaps Budyko's runaway had happened after all. Kirschvink called the idea "snowball Earth," and he also proposed a way out of Budyko's trap. On a frozen planet, volcanoes would keep releasing carbon dioxide into the air. Normally, rain and the weathering of rock gradually remove that gas, but with the continents buried in ice and the oceans sealed beneath it, there would be almost nothing to take it out. Over millions of years, carbon dioxide would build up until the greenhouse effect grew strong enough to melt the ice. Once melting began, the same feedback that had frozen the planet would run in reverse, darkening the surface and speeding the thaw.

Later in the 1990s, the geologist Paul Hoffman and his colleagues found evidence that seemed to fit this scenario remarkably well. In Namibia, directly on top of the glacial deposits, lay thick layers of carbonate rock, the kind that typically forms in warm, shallow seas. An abrupt shift from glacial debris to warm-water sediment was just what one would expect if a carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere had rapidly melted a frozen world.

Not everyone was persuaded. The strongest objection came from life itself. Photosynthetic organisms, including algae, existed before the glaciations and survived them. If the oceans had been covered by thick ice for millions of years, critics asked, how could anything that depends on sunlight have survived? Some researchers have proposed a "slushball" Earth instead, in which a band of open or thinly frozen water remained near the equator. Defenders of the original idea reply that life could have held on in cracks in the ice, around hot springs, or beneath thin, clear ice near volcanic islands.

The debate continues, but it has already changed the questions scientists ask. Budyko treated a frozen Earth as a one-way door, and he used that assumption to rule out the possibility altogether. Kirschvink's insight was that the door might swing both ways. Whether or not the oceans froze completely, it now seems that Earth's climate can lurch between extremes once thought impossible, and that the planet's own processes, given enough time, may be capable of pulling it back.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?

choices.A: A narrator describes the many difficulties of running a small piano-tuning business.
choices.B: A narrator who starts a summer job reluctantly comes to understand and share in the work.
choices.C: A narrator recalls a conflict with an aunt that ends when one of them apologizes.
choices.D: A narrator explains, step by step, the technical process of tuning an old piano.

candidates.evidence: for the first time I heard it
candidates.explanation: The narrator begins bored and reluctant and ends hearing the beats and tuning a note, a change prepared by the visit to Mr. Okafor.

A.rationale: The passage never discusses running the business.

C.rationale: There is no open conflict and no apology.

D.rationale: Tuning is described only in passing; the focus is the narrator's change.

hints: How does the narrator feel at the start and at the end?

strategy.explanation: Compare the first and last paragraphs.

candidates.remember: A narrative's main idea usually involves a change.

candidates.stem: In the first paragraph, the narrator's statement "I let everyone know it" mainly suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: openly complained about having to spend the summer working.
choices.B: was proud of being trusted with Ines's tools.
choices.C: had already told friends about Ines's skill.
choices.D: stopped complaining once the job had begun.

candidates.evidence: I had imagined spending those months at the community pool
candidates.explanation: "It" refers to the narrator's wish to be at the pool instead; letting everyone know shows open complaint.

B.rationale: The narrator is unhappy, not proud, and the tools come later.

C.rationale: "It" refers to the narrator's plans for the pool, not Ines's skill.

D.rationale: The narrator says they were bored for two weeks.

candidates.remember: Read pronouns back to what they refer to.

candidates.stem: Ines's reaction after playing a chord in the church basement (paragraph 2) most strongly suggests that she:

choices.A: was in pain from carrying the heavy tool bag down the stairs.
choices.B: disliked having to work on pianos that belonged to churches.
choices.C: doubted that the old piano could be repaired at all.
choices.D: could hear flaws in the piano's sound that the narrator could not.

candidates.evidence: To me it sounded like a piano
candidates.explanation: Ines winces at a chord that sounds normal to the narrator, showing that she hears problems the narrator cannot.

A.rationale: The narrator carries the bag, and the wince is compared to pain only figuratively.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests she objects to churches.

C.rationale: She goes straight to work on it, which suggests she thought it could be fixed.

hints: How does the narrator's reaction compare with Ines's?
candidates.remember: Contrasts between characters often reveal their traits.

candidates.stem: Ines's explanation for tearing the covers off her books (paragraph 3) is most similar to which of her other actions in the passage?

choices.A: Eating the same sandwich of cheese and pickles at lunch every day
choices.B: Spending nearly two hours tuning a piano that no one in the house played
choices.C: Leaving the narrator to hear the beats without explaining what they would sound like
choices.D: Using only one of the dozen tuning forks that she owned

candidates.evidence: she didn't like being told what to expect
candidates.explanation: Ines dislikes being told what to expect, and she likewise lets the narrator discover the beats without describing them in advance.

A.rationale: This is a habit, but it has nothing to do with not being told what to expect.

B.rationale: This reflects her care for listeners, not a dislike of being told what to expect.

D.rationale: This detail is not connected to knowing what to expect.

hints: What does Ines avoid when she tears off the covers?

strategy.explanation: State the principle, then find another action with the same principle.

candidates.remember: Look for actions that share an underlying reason.

author_checklist.hardness: requires abstracting a principle and matching it across paragraphs

candidates.stem: Mr. Okafor's statement "I like to know it's ready" (paragraph 4) most nearly suggests that he:

choices.A: values having the piano cared for even though he does not play it.
choices.B: plans to begin taking piano lessons soon.
choices.C: expects guests who will want to play it.
choices.D: is preparing the piano to be sold.

candidates.evidence: His piano was old but well cared for
candidates.explanation: He keeps the piano tuned and well cared for in memory of his wife's playing, though he does not play himself.

B.rationale: He says he does not play, and no lessons are mentioned.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests a sale; he keeps it well cared for.

hints: What do you know about who plays this piano?

strategy.explanation: Combine his statement with the details around it.

candidates.stem: When Ines says "That's someone playing it" (paragraph 5), she most nearly means that:

choices.A: Mr. Okafor secretly plays the piano when he has no visitors.
choices.B: Mr. Okafor's careful listening gives the piano a use worth her full effort.
choices.C: the piano is still played by students of Mr. Okafor's wife.
choices.D: the narrator should learn to play the piano before tuning one.

candidates.explanation: Ines answers the question about why she spent so long: because Mr. Okafor listens, the piano is, in a sense, being played, so it deserves careful tuning.

A.rationale: He says he does not play; Ines is not speaking literally.

D.rationale: She is explaining her effort, not advising the narrator.

strategy.explanation: Read the question the narrator asked first.

candidates.remember: A character's answer must fit the question asked.

author_checklist.hardness: figurative statement with a literal trap

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the narrator first heard the beats when:

choices.A: Ines struck two keys together on the piano in the church basement.
choices.B: Ines played a slow piece for Mr. Okafor after finishing her work.
choices.C: handing Ines mutes and felt strips during the first two weeks.
choices.D: striking a tuning fork and a key on the practice piano in Ines's garage.

candidates.evidence: for the first time I heard it
candidates.explanation: In paragraph 6, the narrator strikes the fork and the key and hears the beats "for the first time."

A.rationale: The narrator says they heard nothing but two notes then.

B.rationale: The narrator does not mention hearing beats then.

C.rationale: The narrator was bored then and heard nothing special.

hints: Where does "for the first time" appear?

strategy.explanation: Locate the moment in the passage.

candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: The comparison of the pulse to "two people walking almost but not quite in step" (paragraph 6) mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that the narrator and Ines have begun to work together as equals.
choices.B: show that the old practice piano had been badly damaged by the damp.
choices.C: describe the slight mismatch between two sounds that the narrator can now hear.
choices.D: explain why Ines preferred to work alone rather than with an assistant.

candidates.evidence: a faint wavering, a slow pulse inside the sound
candidates.explanation: The image of two people slightly out of step describes the beats produced when two pitches are slightly different.

A.rationale: The image describes a sound, not the two characters' relationship.

B.rationale: The damp wall was in the church basement, not the garage.

D.rationale: The comparison says nothing about Ines's preferences.

strategy.explanation: Identify what the image refers to.

candidates.remember: Figurative language usually clarifies something nearby.

candidates.stem: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that Ines:

choices.A: was paying closer attention to the narrator's tuning than she seemed to be.
choices.B: had lost interest in her book because she had guessed its ending.
choices.C: disapproved of the way the narrator had turned the tuning pin.
choices.D: wanted the narrator to stop working so that she could read quietly.

candidates.evidence: she had stopped turning the pages
candidates.explanation: Ines appears to be reading, but she has stopped turning the pages, which suggests she was listening to the narrator's work.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests she guessed the ending.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests disapproval; the pulse vanished as it should.

D.rationale: She has stopped reading, not been disturbed in it.

hints: Why might someone holding a book stop turning its pages?

strategy.explanation: Contrast what she seems to do with what she does.

candidates.remember: Small actions can reveal what a character is really doing.

candidates.stem: Compared with the narrator in paragraph 3, the narrator in paragraph 6 is more:

choices.A: eager to rejoin friends at the community pool.
choices.B: critical of the methods Ines uses in her work.
choices.C: impatient with Ines's habit of saying little.
choices.D: engaged in the work of tuning a piano.

candidates.evidence: I turned the pin a fraction, and the pulse slowed
candidates.explanation: In paragraph 3 the narrator watches the clock; in paragraph 6 the narrator tunes a note and listens closely.

A.rationale: The narrator no longer mentions the pool.

B.rationale: The narrator adopts her methods rather than criticizing them.

C.rationale: The narrator does not complain about her silence.

hints: What is the narrator doing in each paragraph?
candidates.remember: Track how a narrator changes across a passage.

candidates.stem: The main function of paragraph 2 is to:

choices.A: show that geologists had already confirmed Budyko's model using evidence from ancient rocks.
choices.B: present geological evidence that the explanations offered at the time did not convincingly explain.
choices.C: explain why most geologists came to accept the idea of a steeply tilted axis.
choices.D: describe the methods geologists use to determine how old a layer of rock is.

candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes glacial deposits near the ancient equator and notes that neither proposed explanation was widely accepted, setting up Kirschvink's answer.

A.rationale: The paragraph does not connect the deposits to Budyko's model or say anything was confirmed.

C.rationale: The paragraph says neither explanation won many converts.

D.rationale: The paragraph mentions the rocks' age but does not explain dating methods.

strategy.explanation: Decide what puzzle the paragraph sets up.

candidates.remember: A paragraph's function often sets up what comes next.

author_checklist.hardness: function in the argument, not content

revision_history.reason: blind solver B: "could not account for" overstated "won few converts"
revision_history.change: key reworded to "did not convincingly explain"
